lawyer:
MI Farooqui with Salimullah, Khurshid Alam Khan and Raziaq Sultana, Advocates --- For the Petitioners in WP Nos. 781/94, 1377/95, 1855, 4893/96 and 79 of 1997.

HR Sharif with Rubaiya Rahman Sharif, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners in WP No. 1472 of 1996.

Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney-General with Mahbub Ali, Assistant Attorney-General ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Karamat Ali and others ------ Petitioners
vs.
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mahfuzur Rahman J: All the writ petitions namely, Writ Petition Nos. 781/94, 1377/95, 1855/96, 4893/96, 79 of 1997 and 1472 of 1996 are taken up together for disposal since in all the cases vires of the Ordinance No.54/85 has been challenged.

<u>2. In all these writ petitions Rules Nisi were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the sub-section (2) of section 5 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance 54 of 1985) should not be declared to be void as being inconsistent with Articles 27 and 42 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. In the aforesaid 5 writ petitions, except Writ Petition No. 1472 of 1996, the judgment and order passed by the First Court of Settlement have been passed without jurisdiction and hence void, illegal and without lawful authority.</u>

<u>3. For the sake of convenience we like to take up the first point regarding the vires of the Ordinance as challenged in the writ petitions. Then we shall decide the next point regarding merit of the individual cases.</u>

<u>4. Mr MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate in all the cases except Writ Petition No. 1472 of 1996 submits that the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 is ultra vires of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh as it offends Articles 27, 31, 48 of our Constitution. Mr Farooqui referring to section 4 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1935 submits that it has been stated therein that in pursuance of a notice in any form issued thereunder at any time before 30th October, 1988 the Government may take over possession of any abandoned property or building. This power of issuing this type of notice in any form gives arbitrary power to the Government and hence it is void ab initio. In support of his contention he referred to the case of Government of Bangladesh vs. Dr Nurul Islam, reported in 33 DLR (AD) 201 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"Since neither the impugned provisions of the Act nor the rules provide any principle or guideline for the exercise of discretion by the Government when it proposes to retire a Government servant from amongst a group of Government servants similarly situated and holding similar jobs, there invariably exists the scope for arbitrary exercise of such discretion.</u>

<u>Discretion of the relevant authority must be seen to have been exercised on some such principles as are discernible in Fundamental Rule 56, Notes 2 of the East Bengal Service Rules and Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants Retirement Rules 1973. Where such basis has been provided the concerned authority before exercising its discretion has to conform to the principles so provided therein."</u>

<u>But this case is not applicable in the present cases as because that was a case regarding retirement of Government employee and there was no guideline or Rules and the facts are also distinguishable. In this regard Mr. Additional Attorney-General submits that Article 25 of President's Order 16 of 1972 clearly provides that the Government may make rules for carrying out the purposes of the order and in exercise of such power Government has framed the notice in the form in exercise of the power vested under Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking over Possession) Rules 1972 and in Rule 6 residential and other buildings in the urban area have been classified as one category of abandoned property. For taking over possession of abandoned property, notice in Forms I, II, III & IV, as, the case may be, can be issued. The learned Additional Attorney-General submits that notice in any form means, depending on the category of abandoned property and notice in any form of the specimen given as per Rule 3 should be issued before taking over of the abandoned property. So, there is no violation of any law and it was nor arbitrary. Mr Farooqui referring to section 4(b) (ii) of Ordinance 54 of 1985 next contends that no building shall be taken possession of as abandoned property under President's Order 16 of 1972 except in pursuance of a notice in any form issued under President's Order 16 of 1972 and where no such notice is issued in respect of a building, in execution of a decree or order passed by a Court in a suit filed by the government. He submits that this is clear discrimination in equality and is hit by equality clause under Articles 27 and 31 of our Constitution. He submits that thereby classification has been made by this Ordinance. He further submits that the Government may institute suit for recovery of abandoned property if those were not included in the list. He next submits that equals are not being treated equally. So, it offends the fundamental right of equality clause as guaranteed under Article 27 of the Constitution. Mr Farooqui then cited a number of decisions but we shall refer only to the relevant ones. In support of his contention he referred the case of Jibendra Kishore Acharyya Chowdhury and 58 others vs. Province of East Pakistan and Secretary, Finance and Revenue Department, Government of East Pakistan, reported in 9 DLR (SC) 21. We have gone through the decision very minutely and find that it is quite distinguishable and the principles, facts and circumstances are not applicable in the present case. He referred to the case of Waris Meah vs. State, reported in PLD 1957 (SC) 157 and submits that establishment of the Court of Settlement by Ordinance 54/85 created discrimination giving right to the government to go to the civil Court for recovery of possession of any abandoned property and debarring the other claimants to establish their claims. In this case it has been held that the Foreign Exchange Regulation(Amendment) Act (XXXII of 1956), which by adding sections 22A, 23(A) and 23B to the original Act gave power to the Central Government or the State Bank to determine whether an offender, under the original Act was to be tried under the ordinary law (section 23), Or by an Adjudication Officer (section 23A), or by a Tribunal (section 23B) and the three sections preserving three different punishing authorities each with different power and procedure and entailing punishments of unequal nature and description, offended against Article 5 of the Constitution and was for that reason void. The amending Act makes the principal Act ex-facie discriminatory and infringes the subject''''s fundamental right to equal protection of the law guaranteed by Article 5 of the Constitution of Pakistan."</u>

<u>In reply the learned Additional Attorney- General submits that the facts of the case are not applicable in the present case as the Government has power to establish such other courts like special courts for disposal of certain cases by proper legislation. He then submits that by section 35 of the Industrial Ordinance the Labour Court has been established, under section 4 of the Family Court Ordinance 1985 Family Court has been established and under section 11 of the Income Tax Ordinance 1984, the Taxes Appellate Tribunal was established. So, the establishment of the Special Court (Settlement Court) for disposal of cases relating to abandoned property is not inconsistent with any provision. Mr Additional Attorney-General has referred the case of Sheikh Abdus Sabur vs. Returning Officer, District Education Officer-in-Charge, Gopalganj and others reported in 41 DLR (AD) 30 re paragraphs 28, 29, 38, 74 and 76 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>28. From the respective submissions of the parties in this case the question before us is whether the guarantee of the Constitution, in Article 27, that "all citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law" has been disregarded in the impugned legislation, namely, section 7(2)(g) of the Union Parishad Ordinance. First of all, it is to be clearly understood what ''''the equality of law'''' means. Sir Ivor Jennings in his "The Law and the Constitution" has stated:</u>

<u>"Equality before the law means that among equals the law should be equal and should be equally administered, that like should be treated alike". Dicey in his "Law of the Constitution" stated: Equality before the law does not mean absolute equality of men which is a physical impossibility, but the denial of any special privileges by reason of birth, creed or the like in favour of any individual and also the equal subjection of all individuals and classes to the ordinary law of the land administered by the ordinary law Courts''''"</u>

<u>5. In the "Limitation of Government Power" by Rotundy and others "Equal protection of the laws" has been described as:</u>

<u>"The equal protection clause guarantees that similar individuals will be dealt with in a similar manner by the government. It does not reject the Government''''s ability to classify, persons or draw lines in creation and application of laws, but it does guarantee that those classifications will not be based upon impermissible criteria or arbitrarily used to burden a group of individuals. Such a classification does not violate the guarantee when it distinguishes persons as ''''dissimilar'''' upon some permissible basis in order to advance the legitimate interest of society.</u>

<u>"In Southern Rly Co. vs. Greene, 216 US 400 Day-J observed:</u>

<u>"Equal protection of the laws means subjection to equal laws, applying like to all in the same Situation."</u>

<u>Chandrachud-J in "Indira Gandhi vs. Raj Narayan", AIR 1975, SC 2279 described his idea of equality as:</u>

<u>"All who are equal are equal in the eye of law", meaning that it will not accord favoured treatment to persons within the same class."</u>

<u>29. On consideration of the views expressed by these distinguished Judges and Authors as to the meaning of the "equality before law" and equal protection of the law". I do not think that I will be able to define this term in a better way, "Equality before law" is not to be interpreted in its absolute sense to hold that all persons are equal in all respects disregarding different conditions and circumstances in which they are placed or special qualities and characteristics which some of them may possess but which are lacking in others. The term protection of ''''equal law'''' is used to mean that all persons or things are not equal in all cases and that persons similarly situated should be treated alike. Equal protection is the guarantee that similar people will be dealt with in a similar way and that people of different circumstances will not be treated as if they were the same, A single law therefore cannot be applied uniformly to all persons disregarding their basic differences with others; and if these differences are identified, then the persons or things may be classified into different categories according to those distinctions; this is what is called ''permissible criteria'' or "intelligible differentia", The Legislature while proceeding to make law with certain object in view, which is either to remove some evil or to confer some benefit, has power to make classification on reasonable basis. Classification of persons for the purpose of legislation is different from class legislation which is forbidden. To stand the test of ''''equality'''' a classification, besides being based on intelligent differentia, must have reasonable nexus with the object the legislature intends to achieve by making the classification. A classification is reasonable if it aims at giving special treatment to a backward section of the population; it is also permissible to deal out distributive justice by taxing the privileged class and subsidizing the poor section of the people. What is of fundamental importance in law-making is that while making a classification the legislature shall not act arbitrarily but make selection on rational basis. In the light of these observations I shall see whether the impugned legislation is supportable in terms of ''equality of law'' within the meaning of Article 27 of the Constitution. In support of their respective contentions learned Counsels have cited many decisions which I now proceed to consider.</u>

<u>38 ..................................................... It also must be presumed that when any law is made it is constitutionally valid until the presumption is rebutted by the person who challenges its validity. The United States Supreme Court in Middleton vs. Texas P & L Co 248 US 152, observed:</u>

<u>"It must be presumed that a Legislature understands and correctly appreciates the needs of its own people, that its laws are directed to problems made manifest by experience and that Its discriminations are based upon adequate grounds."</u>

<u>Bruen J in Gulf Colorado Rly vs. Ellis, 165 US 150, however, warned against carrying this presumption too far and observed:</u>

<u>"To carry the presumption to the extent of holding that there must be some undisclosed and unknown reason for subjecting certain individual or corporations to hostile and discriminatory legislation is to make the protection clause of the 14th Amendment a mere rope of sand."</u>

<u>Bhagawati J. in Shujat Ali vs. Union of India AIR 1974, SC 1631 observed:</u>

<u>"The doctrine of classification should not be carried to a point where instead of being a useful servant it becomes a dangerous master."</u>

<u>In Lachmon Das vs. State of Punjab (Supra) Subha Rao J observed:</u>

<u>"Over-emphasis on the doctrine of classification or an anxious and sustained attempt to find some basis for classification may gradually and imperceptibly deprive the article of its glorious content. That process would gradually and imperceptibly substitute the doctrine of classification for the doctrine of equality".</u>

<u>74. In the same vein Bhagawati, J said in the case of Sakhawat AU AIR 1955 (SC) 166:</u>

<u>“.................. at egis anon enacted in the achievement of a particular object or purpose need not be all embracing. It is for the legislature to determine what categories it would embrace within the scope of legislation and merely because certain categories which would stand on the same footing as those which are covered by the legislation are left out would not render legislation which has been enacted in any manner discriminatory and violative, of the fundamental right guaranteed by Article 14 of the Constitution."</u>

<u>76. A law cannot be struck down merely because it fails to spell out the particular objective of provision in the legislation itself. In the instant case the impugned clause (g) was brought in by the Local Government Laws (Amendment) Act 1997 (Act XXIII of 1987) apparently for the purpose of providing an additional ''''disqualification'''' for a person seeking election to an Union Parishad. For the purpose of withstanding a challenge to its constitutionality as being violative of Article 27 it was to stand the test of justification for being attached to Local Government body election only.And for that to begin with, item 7 of the propositions as above will be attracted ie the court ill presume the Constitutionality of a Statute until shown otherwise, Bhagwati, J in the case of R K Garg vs. Union of India AIR 1951 (SC) 2138 , reiterated that" the presumption of constitutionality is indeed so strong that in order to sustain it, the Court may take into consideration matters of common knowledge, matters of common report, the history of the times and may assume every state of facts which can be conceived existing at the time of legislation."</u>

<u>Relying on these decisions the learned Additional Attorney-General submits that it must be presumed that law is made consistent and valid unless the presumption is rebutted. He then submits that the Settlement Court was created for disposal of certain classes of cases relating to abandoned properties speedily and there is no violation of any rules or law and also there is no unreasonable classification amongst the owners within the area.</u>

<u>6. Mr Farooqui next contends that Ordinance 54/85 was made operative from 28th November, 1985 making provisions exclusively for the residential buildings or other buildings or structures of any kind in an urban area and thus excluded the residential buildings and other properties outside the urban area. In reply Mr Additional Attorney-General submits that in view of section 3 of the Ordinance there is no discrimination because the law is prospective in nature. Mr Farooqui next referred the case of CQMH Md Ayub Ali vs. Bangladesh and others, reported in 47 DLR (AD) 71 relevant paragraph 33 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"…………………That fact that building is included in the list is proof of its being an abandoned property section 5(2) and the Government has nothing to prove or deny. It is for the aggrieved person to establish his claim by whatever evidence he chooses to produce. The denial of a fair trial will only arise if a proper opportunity is not afforded to the person for producing his evidence or any evidence sought to be adduced by him is unreasonably shut out or he is not given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. A Court of Settlement under section 10(5) is obliged to make such enquiry as it may deem necessary and give reasonable opportunity to the parties concerned of being heard and to produce evidence, both oral and documentary, if any."</u>

<u>He also referred to the case of Government of Bangladesh vs. Md Jalil and others reported in 15 BLD (AD) 175 relevant paragraph 14 wherein it has been held that:</u>

<u>"14. The High Court Division, in our opinion, started with a wrong premise holding that the presumption of correctness of the entries in the Gazette Notification does not absolve the Government from denying the facts alleged by the claimant or from disclosing the  basis of treating ,the property as abandoned property when it is disputed. Section 5(2) of the Ordinance clearly provides that the list published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government, as such, section 7 says that a person claiming any right or interest in any such building may make an application to the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the building from such list, etc. on the ground that the building is not an abandoned building and has not vested in the Government under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 or that his right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of that order. The onus, therefore, is squarely on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the properly as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant"</u>

<u>He next referred the case of Rahima Begum and others vs. Court of Settlement and others, reported in 17 BLD (AD) 118 = 2 BLC (AD) 108 relevant paragraph 7 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"Once a building is included in the list of abandoned properties it is conclusive, evidence that the building in question is an abandoned property where the owner either was not present in Bangladesh or his whereabouts were not known or he eased to manage or occupy the property at the time when President's Order 16 of 1972 was promulgated on 16-2-1972. This presumption is, of course, a rebuttable one. It is for the claimant to show that the original owner was present in Bangladesh or his whereabouts were known or he did not cease to occupy or manage the property in question at the relevant time. Since the notification in the official Gazette carries a presumption that the building in question is in abandoned property, it is exempt from any legal process be it an auction sale by the Government itself or through court"</u>

<u>He next referred the case of Rasheeda Begum vs. Government of Bangladesh, reported in 2 BLC (AD) 158 relevant paragraphs 9 and 11 wherein it has been held :</u>

<u>"9. Admittedly, the property has been listed as an abandoned property. Thus the onus lies upon the petitioner to the but the presumption, provided in sub-section (2) of sections 5 that the same was not an abandoned property. No oral evidence has been adduced before the Settlement Court to prove that on 26-2-72 when President''''s Order 16 of 1972 was promulgated the original lessee, Naimuddin had been present in Bangladesh or his whereabouts were known or that he did not cease to occupy, supervise or manage in person the house in question. The Settlement Court upon assigning cogent reasons held that the kabala of the petitioner's vendor is a forged and fabricated document and the original lessee, Naimuddin did never appear physically before any authority for any purpose after the liberation war in Bangladesh. The High Court Division has thus, rightly, maintained the order of the Settlement Court by the impugned judgment and order.</u>

<u>11. In a number of cases we have already decided that enlistment of a building under section 5 of the Ordinance shall retain its position as an abandoned property, in view of the provision of sub-section (2) thereof, unless the presumption is rebutted that the same. is not an abandoned property within the meaning of Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972".</u>

<u>7. Mr Additional Attorney-General submits that it is clear from these decisions referred to that once the property is listed as abandoned property it must be presumed that Government has formed opinion regarding abandoned character of the property as defined in Article 2 of the President's Order 16 of 1972 and by the aforesaid decisions their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that if once it is listed it is presumed that it has been correctly listed as abandoned property. After careful reading of the decisions referred above of the Appellate Division we are of the view that there is no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners in this respect.</u>

<u>8. Mr HR Sharif, the learned Advocate appearing in Writ Petition No. 1472 of 1996 adopted the submissions made by Mr Farooqui in this regard.</u>

<u>9. We have carefully gone through the relevant provision of President's Order 16 of 1972, the Rules framed thereunder, the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 and also the cases referred to above, and we are of the view that there is no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners.</u>

<u>Writ Petition No. 781 of 1994.</u>

10. In Writ Petition No. 781 of 1994 the case of the petitioner is as follows:

The petitioner who was born in Bihar, India was in service of the then British India as a fireman. After partition on 14-8-47 he migrated to the then East Pakistan as an Optee Employee and joined the then East Pakistan Fire Service in 1947 and posted at Lalmonirhat as a Fireman and retired from the Government Employment on December 16, 1991. The petitioner purchased the case land under PS Lalmonirhat, District Rangpour by two deeds of conveyance being Nos. 6507 and 10276 dated 14-10-64 and 14-6-68 respectively and was in possession of the same. While he was in peaceful possession the Government evicted him in early 1972 and thereafter he made several representations but to no effect and ultimately on 10-8-96 he filed an application under section 7 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985. It is stated that the petitioner is a citizen of Bangladesh and he retired from Government Service in 1971 and has been receiving pension from the Government as a retired fireman. So, the inclusion of his property as abandoned property is illegal and without any lawful authority and the property does not come within the mischief of the definition of abandoned property and violative to the fundamental right guaranteed by our Constitution.

11. The Settlement Court after hearing by its judgment and order dated 3-3-94 dismissed the application.

12. As against that the petitioner moved this court and obtained this Rule.

13. The Government opposes the Rule but did not file any affidavit-in-opposition."

14. Mr MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the petitioner is a Bangladeshi National and he never abandoned the property in question but temporarily hid himself for the safety of his life and he retired from Government service in the year 1971. After liberation of Bangladesh he moved the authority for release of the house from the list of the abandoned property but could not succeed. Thereafter as soon as the Settlement Court was set up he filed an application under section 7 of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. The petitioner's pension book has been filed and it appears that he drew Taka 63.08 paisa as pension per month and. Taka 3363.20 as gratuity was allowed. It further appears that by an order of the District Accounts Officer, Rangpur dated 25-11-80 the petitioner was allowed to draw pension from 16th December, 1971 upto July, 1982 ie 126 months 16 days at a time. He submits that during the absence of the petitioner the house in possession was declared abandoned under President's Order 16 of 1972 and given in possession of an employee of fire service department. There is nothing to show that Government ever formed any opinion that he was absent and acted prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh thereby because he was not found in possession of the property it cannot be declared abandoned. He submits that section 2 of the President's Order 16 of 1972 does not provide for inclusion of such property in the list of abandoned buildings as defined in section 2(1) of President's Order 16 of 1972. He submits that the Settlement Court acted without jurisdiction in dismissing the petition of the petitioner.

15. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Additional Attorney-General, opposes the Rule but did not file any affidavit-in-opposition refuting the assertions of the petitioner.

16. We have perused the impugned judgment and order. True in a writ of certiorari we cannot look into the facts of claim and counter claim. Section 2 of President's Order 16 of 1972 sub-section 1(i) (a) defined "abandoned property" as any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971 was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People''''s Republic of Bangladesh but did not include any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh;

It is not denied that the petitioner purchased the disputed property and was in possession of the same since purchase on 14-10-64 and got his name mutated and paid rent up to 1986 in Miscellaneous Case No. 1019/76-77. He also filed the Nationality Certificate dated 30-4-77 issued by Pourashava Commissioner, Syedpur. An Affidavit sworn before a Magistrate on 27-4-86 has been filed to show petitioners allegiance to Bangladesh. He also submitted the voter list of the area to show that the name of the petition and other members of his family appear in the list as voters. All these facts and Government records clearly indicate that he is a citizen of Bangladesh. But it appears the learned Court of Settlement without considering this aspect rejected the petitioner on mere conjecture and surmises without any finding that the aforesaid records are forged. We find from the impugned judgment that the court held that'''' out of the petitioner's claim for 21 decimals of land he filed a kabala covering only 13½ decimals of land and he did not file any document for the remaining land claimed by him whereas both the documents were filed before the Court of Settlement but the Settlement Court did not take into consideration the other document covering the remaining land. The conclusiveness of proof of abandoned property as defined in section 5(2) of Ordinance 54/85 is rebuttable presumption as was held by their Lordships in the case of Bangladesh vs. Ashraf Ali reported in 49 DLR (AD) 161 relevant paragraph 8.

"No rebuttable evidence could be adduced to show that original owner Yahiya was present in Bangladesh and he occupied, managed or supervised the disputed building when President's Order 16 of 1972 came into operation. Hence, the listing of the property as an abandoned property in the Supplementary Provisions Ordinance, 1985 was lawful as it was ail abandoned property by operation of law."

<u>17. In view of the discussions made above, we are of the view that the petitioner has adduced sufficient evidence and materials to show that he is the owner of the property and he occupied, managed and supervised the same except for a short period when he took shelter elsewhere for safety of his life.</u>

<u>18. In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No. 759 of 1992 is hereby set aside and the property is question is excluded from the list of the abandoned property as described in Column C. The authority concerned is further directed to hand over vacant possession of the same to the petitioner preferably within 60 days from the date of receipt of this order.</u>

Writ Petition No. 1377 of 1995

19. In this writ petition the case of the petitioner is that, the property belonged to Rafi Ahmed Fidai who got the same by way of allotment from the then Government of East Pakistan. Rafi Ahmed Fidai sold the suit land to Mrs Jakia Khatoon at Taka 8000.00 on 6-6-63 and Jakia Khatoon sold the suit property again in favour of the petitioner Mrs Ambia Khatoon for Taka 12000.00 by executing a deed of sale on 21-2-74 and registered the same on 18-4-74. Jakia Khatoon paid Municipal taxes and the petitioner while living in the suit property after purchase used to pay electricity bills, gas charges, Wasa bills and the draft of RS record in respect of the suit property has been prepared in the name of the applicant. The further case of the petitioner is that the provisions of the Ordinance No. 54/85 have no manner of application as the petitioner was in possession and no notice was served upon the petitioner. So, the inclusion of the case property under section 5(i)(b) was illegal. The Settlement Court by its judgment and order dated 20-12-94 dismissed the case of the petitioner.

20. As against that the petitioner moved this court and obtained this Rule.

21. Mr MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the property in question has been illegally enlisted as abandoned property in clear violation of the provisions of law and, as such, the enlistment of the same is illegal and ultra vires. By supplementary affidavit the petitioner introduced certain facts without any materials on record.

22. The Government appeared and opposed the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition denying all material allegations and stated that the document in favour of Zakia Khatoon alleged to have been executed by Rafi Ahmed Fidai on 6-6-63 were forged, null and void and mere paper transaction and I has been created by false personation and the signature of Rafi Ahmad Fidai does not tally with the signature of Rafi Ahmed Fidai in the alleged sale deed. The sale deed alleged to have been executed by Zakia Khatoon in favour of the petitioner on 21-3-74 is also void, inoperative, without consideration and a paper transaction and the same is hit by Article 6 of President''''s Order 16 of 1972. Furthermore, the LTI is quite different from the LTI of Zakia Khatoon and Zakia Khatoon had no existence and her name was never mutated with the Housing and Settlement Department. It is stated that Rafi Ahmad Fidai never transferred the property to Zakia Khatoon or anybody else. Rafi Ahmad Fidai was a non-local and during liberation war his whereabouts were not known and he ceased to manage, occupy and supervise the case property in person, hence the property was rightly vested in the Government as abandoned under President''''s Order 16 of 1972.

23. The petitioner filed affidavit-in-reply reiterating the contents of the petition.

<u>24. We find that the Settlement Court upon consideration of oral and documentary evidence came to the finding that Zakia Khatoon, the vendor of the petitioner, was a fake person who did not purchase the land from original owner Rafi Ahmed Fidal. Zakia Khatoon was not examined in this case before the Court of Settlement and no evidence came before the court that Zakia Khatoon died and Settlement Court also found that L TI of Zakia Khatoon in the first page of the Kabala executed in favour of Ambia Khatoon does not tally with LTI in the rest of the pages and the expert opined in the similar way. The Settlement Court also came to a finding that the fact that Zakia Khatoon was a fictitious person. So the question of purchase of the case property by Jakia Khatoon on 6th June, 1963 does not arise. Accordingly, the purchase of the case property by the present petitioner from her does not arise. Her kabala and the kabala in the name of Jakia are products of false personation. All these are findings of fact and in a petition of certiorari we cannot look into it. The findings of the Court of Settlement are based on facts and materials produced before it. This court could interfere with the findings of fact under its jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution only if it could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence and facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it had acted malafide or in violation of any principle of natural justice. In the case of Mostafa Kamal (Md) vs. First Court of Settlement and others, reported in 48 DLR (AD) 61 relevant paragraph 4 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"4. Court of Settlement on consideration of the materials on record arrived at a finding that Nasima Khatun is not the daughter and heir of original lessee Mobina Khatun and that the said lessee had not been in possession of the house in question at the relevant time. The learned Judges of the High Court Division upon taking into consideration of such clear finding of facts of the Court of Settlement refused rightly to interfere with the judgment of that court upon a correct appreciation of the legal principle that the High Court Division in exercise of its writ jurisdiction can not sit as a Court of Appeal over the judgment of the Court of Settlement for resettling questions of fact. Thus we find no illegality in the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division."</u>

<u>In the case of Bangladesh vs. Ashraf Ali @ Ashraf Ali, reported in 49 DLR (AD) 161 relevant paragraph 6 wherein it has been held:</u>

<u>"6…………………..In exercising the jurisdiction in certiorari the learned Judges sat over the judgment of the Tribunal as a court of appeal and reversed the findings of fact of the Court of Settlement. The learned Judges on consideration of the materials and evidences on record took a different view that Md Nasim was the son of original allottee Yahiya as the original title deed and original receipts showing payment of rent, taxes, etc. were produced from the custody of respondent No. 1. The learned Judges relied very much on this circumstantial evidence. The learned Judges also found that respondent No.1 having failed to give the exact date of death does not ipso facto disprove the assertion that Yahiya died some time in 1970.</u>

<u>The manner in which the learned Judges considered the materials on record is in fact the manner in which a court of appeal disposes of an appeal. The learned Judges of the High Court Division exceeded their jurisdiction while exercising their power under certiorari to interfere with the judgment of an inferior tribunal.</u>

25. In view of the discussions made above, we are of the view that there is nothing to interfere and the property in question has rightly been enlisted as abandoned property.

26. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. Writ Petition No. 1855 of 1996.

27. By this Writ Petition No. 1855 of 1996 the petitioner challenged the impugned order dated 2-3-96 passed by the Settlement Court No. 1 in Case No. 863 of 1987 as illegal and of no legal effect.

28. The case of the petitioner is that, the case property consisting of 2 storied building previously belonged to one Md Humayun Mirza by virtue of purchase from Md Kashem on 21-6-63. The said purchaser executed power of attorney in favour of Anisur Rahman and got it registered on 24-3-73 and thereby appointed Anisur Rahman to manage the property and sell out same on his behalf, if necessary. Humayun Mirza started a hotel in the case property in the year 1974 on obtaining permission of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka. Thereafter he sold the property to Nuruzzaman by a registered kabala dated 10-3-73 and delivered possession to the purchaser. The purchaser Md Nuruzzaman mortgaged the property with the Pubali Bank for taking loan. Thereafter Md Nuruzzaman executed a bainapatra in favour of the petitioner Abu Naser Siddique on 19-9-78 for sale of the case property for a consideration of Taka 1,60,000.00. The vendor Nuruzzaman received Taka 50,000.00 as advance but did not execute kabala. Again Nazrnul Huq, brother of Nuruzzaman, executed another bainapatra on behalf of his brother on 18-10-78 and received Taka 1,00,000.00. The petitioner filed Title Suit No. 1262 of 1980 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against Nuruzzaman for specific performance of contract and the suit was decreed ex parte on 16-1-83. In pursuance of the ex parte decree, the petitioner got kabala executed and registered through court on 9-7-86 and in this way the petitioner has become owner of the property but it has been wrongly treated as abandoned property performance of contract and the suit was decreed ex parte on 16-1-83. In pursuance of the ex parte decree, the petitioner got kabala executed and registered through court on 9-7-86 and in this way the petitioner has become owner of the property but it has been wrongly treated as abandoned property.

30. As against that the petitioner moved this Court and obtained this Rule.

31. Mr MI Farooqui the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the Court of Settlement, on a wrong interpretation and construction of law relating to citizenship, committed an error of law in finding that Mirza Humayun, the admitted original owner, is a citizen of a State which was at war and engaged in military operation against Bangladesh during the war of liberation. He next contends that the property, from the facts and evidence adduced on behalf of the petitioner, is not an abandoned property. The settlement court erred in law in not excluding it from the abandoned list.

32. Respondent No. 1 contested the petition  by filing an affidavit-in-opposition denying all material allegations made in the petition contending, inter alia; that Md Nuruzzaman never purchased the case property from Humayun Mirza and created a collusive sale deed dated 10-3-76 through Anisur Rahman who was alleged to have been appointed and legally nominated attorney of Humayun Mirza in 1973 or that Humayun Mirza was not in Bangladesh at the relevant time who was a non-local and left the country as a citizen of Pakistan. During liberation war and afterwards whereabouts of said Humayun Mirza were not known and he ceased to manage, occupy and supervise the case property in person and was a citizen of a State which was engaged in military operations against Bangladesh and hence the case property vested in the Government as abandoned property under President's Order 16 of 1972. The alleged sale deeds are null and void, inoperative, false, forged and without consideration and mere paper transaction. It is further stated that the so-called power of attorney dated 24-12-73 Annexure-A and Al are false, fraudulent, forged and fabricated documents and never acted upon. It is further submitted that at the relevant time since Mirza Humayun was not a citizen of Bangladesh the property was correctly enlisted as abandoned property under President's Order 16 of 1972.

33. The petitioner filed a reply to the affidavit-in-opposition reiterating the averments made in the writ petition.

34. We have carefully gone through the impugned judgment and order of the Settlement Court which on consideration of both, the oral and documentary evidence found that the petitioner has not been able to satisfy the court that Humayun Mirja was a Bangladeshi citizen at the relevant time and stayed in this country till the transfer of the property by his alleged constituted attorney Anisur Rahman which took place on 10-3-76. The Settlement Court also found that the name of Humayun Mirza was not also recorded in the voter list and there is no proof to show that he was a national of Bangladesh. So the Settlement Court rightly found that he was not available in the country. Even Md Nuruzzaman who deposed as PW 1 could not say whether Humayun Mirza obtained the citizenship of Bangladesh and could not say where he went. The Settlement Court also found on perusal of the Government file that an inquiry was made in this respect and it was found that the owner of the case house Humayun Mirza left this country and settled in Pakistan and at that time it was detected that the occupants of the house were trespassers in the abandoned property.

It is asserted by the petitioner that he obtained an ex parte decree with respect to the suit property and became the owner. In the case of CQMH Md Ayub Ali vs. Bangladesh and others, reported in 47 DLR (AD) 71 relevant paragraph 26 wherein it has been held:

"The decree in the suit for specific performance of contract will show that it has only decided the controversy between the vendor and the vendee and directed the vendor to execute the necessary document in favour of the vendee. Such a decree is not the one which is mentioned in Proviso (a) and, as such, the existence of such a decree cannot be pleaded as a bar for inclusion of the building in the list."

<u>35. Furthermore, it appears that the facts are inconsistent. Once it is said by the petitioner that he obtained a bainapara from Anisur Rahman the alleged consituted attorney of Humayun Mirza and again asserted that he obtained bainapatra from Nazmul Huq also and the ex parte decree in question was obtained against both of them. So no reliance can be placed on the ex parte decree. These are all disputed questions of fact <u>The averments made in the petition are questions of fact which cannot be looked into by this court in a petition of certiorari. In the case of Bangladesh vs. Ashraf Ali, reported in 49 DLR (AD) 161 relevant para 6 wherein their Lordships have held:</u></u>

<u>"6....... In exercising the jurisdiction in certiorari the learned Judges sat over the judgment of the Tribunal as a court of appeal and reversed the findings of facts of the Court of Settlement The learned Judges on consideration of the materials and evidences on record took a different view that Md Nasim was the son of original allottee Yahiya as the original title deed and original receipts showing payment of rent, taxes, etc. were produced from the custody of respondent No. 1. The learned Judges relied very much on this circumstantial evidence. The learned Judges also found that respondent No.1 having failed to give the exact date of death does not ipso facto disprove the assertion that Yahiya died some time in 1970. The manner in which the learned Judges considered the material on record is, in fact, the manner in which a court of appeal disposes of an appeal. The learned Judges of the High Court Division exceeded their jurisdiction while exercising their power under certiorari to interfere with the judgment of an inferior tribunal."</u>

36. In view of the discussions and the decisions referred above we are of the view there is nothing to interfere in the matter.

37. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement is hereby affirmed.

Writ Petition No. 4893 of 1996,

<u>"6…………………..In exercising the jurisdiction in certiorari the learned Judges sat over the judgment of the Tribunal as a court of appeal and reversed the findings of fact of the Court of Settlement. Writ Petition No.1472 of 1996

56. By this Writ Petition No. 1472 of 1996 the petitioner challenged the vires of the law which we have discussed earlier and given our decision. Without approaching the Settlement Court the petitioner directly came to this court challenging the inclusion of the property in the list of the abandoned property against item No. 4 in ''''Kha'''' list vide Gazette Notification dated 23-9-86 prepared pursuant to Ordinance No. 54 of 1985.

The case of the petitioners is that, Mrs. Amina Khatun predecessor-in-interest of the petitioner, obtained 99 years leasehold right along with the possession of the plot No. CES(b) CYC 284 Road No.117 from the Dhaka Improvement Trust with such terms and conditions as described in the standard lease agreement dated 17-3-61 upon payment of full consideration amount. A photo copy of the said receipt of the petitioners of the said amount as transfer fee is annexed hereto and marked as Annexure-''C''. On completion of all legal formalities the petitioners obtained the deed of sale from the original lessee on 28-2-73. By supplementary affidavit the petitioners asserted that while the petitioners came to  learn in early part of April, 1996 that the   property had been listed in the ''Kha'' list as aforesaid, the petitioners together with Mr Khandker Mojibur Rahman, husband of the petitioner No.1, went to the Settlement Court No. 1, Dhaka on 8-4-96 for filing a case to release the property from the list of abandoned building but they were informed by the Registrar of the said Settlement Court that since the time to file such case had expired long ago the Settlement Court would not accept any new case. Whereupon the petitioners solicited advice of Sharif and Nabi, Advocates who advised for filing a writ petition. The copies of the letters of the Pubali Bank are annexed herewith and marked as Annexures- K and K-1.

58. Respondent No. 1 contested the petition by filing an affidavit-in-opposition denying all  material assertions contending, inter alia that the original owner Amena Khatun left this country prior to promulgation of President's Order 16 of 1972 and left the property uncared for arid her whereabouts were not known. So the alleged sale deed dated 28-2-73 is a false and concocted one and was created in order to grab the valuable properties' of the Government. It is also stated in the affidavit-in-opposition that since the petitioners are not the owners of the property no notice was required to be served upon them since the original owner left the country keeping the property uncared for and ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person the property and the property was rightly declared as abandoned. It is further stated that Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 is a beneficial legislation and very much constitutional. It is further stated that this Writ Petition is not maintainable as because the Court of Settlement has got exclusive jurisdiction to adjudicate the matter-relating to exclusion of the property from abandoned list and since the petitioner had never gone to the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the property from the list of abandoned property as provided under Ordinance 54 of 1985 the instant Writ Petition is not maintainable. It. is further stated that the petitioner has never gone to the Court of Settlement to seek redress inasmuch as nobody is required to go to the Registrar of the Court of Settlement for filing cases, as the functions of the Registrar do not relate to filing of cases, rather the function of the registrar is administrative in nature.

59. Mr. HR Sharif, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that the petitioners came to learn in the early part of April, 1996 that the property in question had been listed in the 'Kha' list. Thereafter as per provision of section 7 of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 to seek redress the petitiones along with Mr Khondker Mojibur Rahman, husband of petitionr No. 1, went to the Court of Settlement, Dhaka on 7-4-86 for filing the case for release of the property from the list of the abandoned building and they were informed by the Registrar of the settlement court that since the specified time to file such case had long expired the Settlement Court would not accept any new case. The learned Advocate submits that he filed the writ petition to this Division under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh for enforcement of his fundamental rights under Part-3 of the Constitution is quite maintainable. Their right to property as guaranteed under Article 42(1) of the Constitution can be enforced by a Writ Petition. He next contends that in spite of the fact that they did not avail of the opportunity of seeking redress in the alternative forum, the Settlement Court, the writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution is very much maintainable. Special forum has been provided under the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 for seeking redress for releasing the property before the Settlement Court within 108 days from the date of publication of the list in the official Gazette which has admittedly expired long back. The learned Advocate submits that for the first time the petitioner came to know about the matter in April, 1986 when Rajuk refused to accord permission for Division of plots amongst the petitioners and by that time the statutory period of limitation for filing an application before the Settlement Court was over. Mr Sharif .submits that this writ petition under Article 102 for enforcement of fundamental right as guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution is quite maintainable. In support of his contention he referred the case of Saleha Khatun vs. Chairman, 1st Court of Settlement and another, reported in, 49 DLR 243 relevant para 6 wherein it has been held:

"The petitioner is entitled to challenge the inclusion of her house in the ''Ka'' list of abandoned buildings by way of the Court's writ jurisdiction of this court in spite of dismissal of her application by the Court of Settlement on the ground of limitation".

He next referred the case of Joban Nahar and others vs. Bangladesh, through the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works Department, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others, reported in 49 DLR 108 paragraph 13 wherein it has been held:

"Ordinarily the Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution will not interfere where there is equally effective and efficacious remedy available to a petitioner. Yet the existence of another remedy is not in every case a bar to the exercise of power of the High Court under Article 102 of the Constitution and the court can interfere if the circumstances demand such interference."

In paragraph 19 it has also been held:

"19………………………….The right to enforce a fundamental right is another fundamental right which gives the petitioner right to move this court even though his application was rejected by the Settlement Court on the ground of limitation."

He then referred the case of Begum Lutfunnessa vs. People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary. Ministry of Works and ors. reported in 42 DLR (AD) 86 relevant page 88 paragraphs 11 and 12 wherein it has been held:

"11. It appears that the High Court Division upon examining the different provisions of the Ordinance including section 7 came to the finding that the said section can give the appellant exactly the same remedy. which she was praying for in the petition, that the Court of Settlement has been given the specific power to exclude the disputed property from the impugned list, that the appellant has been given specific right to argue before the Court of Settlement that the building is not an abandoned property, that it has not vested in the government and that her right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of President's Order 16 of 1972. When the Statute has devised Ian alternative forum for giving complete relief to the appellant, the learned Judges observed, she could not invoke the writ jurisdiction without exhausting the remedy provided for in the Ordinance".

12. That aforesaid view taken by the High, Court Division generally speaking, is well in accord with the settled principle governing exercise of discretionary jurisdiction under Article 102 of the , Constitution when the law itself provides for a remedy which is sought for in the writ petition. We therefore, have no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment on the ground that any principle has been laid down which can not be justified. Even so the facts of the present case as revealed are such that it is found plainly difficult to sustain the ultimate order refusing to interfere with the impugned notification. It will be seen that section 5 (1)(a) of the Ordinance under which the impugned notification was published authorises the government to publish in the Official Gazette (a) a list of buildings the possession of which has been taken as abandoned property under the President's Order (President's Order No. 16 of 1972). The minimum the Government must show in a proceeding where the publication of the list is challenged in respect of any property by its owner, is that the property has at some point of time been taken possession of as abandoned property. In the instant case there appears to be no dear assertion made by the respondents as to when the disputed house was taken over by the Government as abandoned property and how the property was being managed by the Government since then. It has been merely asserted by the respondents that during and  after the liberation struggle the whereabouts of the  owner of the house were not known and the  government rightly enlisted the property as abandoned property, that the appellant was never in possession of the house and that it was occupied by the SP Dhaka and it is being presently used as Police Box and Office."

He next contends that the inclusion of the property in ''Kha'' list was without any legal basis as no notice was served upon the petitioners. Mr Sharif   submits that admittedly no notice has been served   upon the petitioners as required under law and   Government did not take possession of the property as abandoned and admittedly the petitioners are still in possession of the same and it is the condition precedent that physical possession of the building must have been taken over by the Government before it could be listed as an abandoned property.

60. He also referred the case of Iqbal Afirhed  Quraishi vs. Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works, Government of the People''''s Republic of Bangladesh, Dhaka, reported in 45 DLR, 416 relevant paragraph 8 wherein it has been held:

"It is condition precedent that the physical possession of the building must have been taken  over by the government before it could be listed  as an abandoned properly."

61. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan. The learned Additional Attorney-General, opposes the Rule by filing affidavit-in- opposition. He submits that this instant writ petition is not maintainable when the petitioners did not avail the alternative forum before the Settlement Court.

62. On the point of maintainability we find that the petition under Article 102 of the Constitution is very much maintainable as the petitioners for the first time came to know about the enlistment of the property in 'Kha' list in the year 1996 when they went to file the application before the Rajuk for partition of the property and by-this time the statutory period of 108 days for filing an application [or release of the property before the Settlement Court was over. It is not denied by the government that the property is still in possession of the petitioners and no notice was served as required under the provision of section 5(i) (b) of Ordinance No. 54/85 which reads as follows:

"Section 5(i)(b) : The Government shall after the 31st day of March, 1986, and before the 30th day of April, 1986 publish in the official Gazette.

(a) a list of buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property under the President's Order:

(b) a list of buildings in respect of which notice for surrendering or taking possession 'as abandoned under the said Order have been issued: Provided …………………………. …………………………………..

Since no notice was served under the aforesaid mandatory provision of the Ordinance 54 of 1985, the petitioners were not aware that the property was included in the 'Kha' list as alleged.

63. It is also not denied by the respondent that Amena Khatoon, original lessee of the plot, was a citizen of erstwhile East Pakistan and at the relevant time and with permission dated 1-1-73 sold the same to the petitioners by a registered deed of sale and she also paid the transfer fee of Taka 6,700.00 in favour of respondent No. 2 Annexure-A' and 'C' respectively. It is also not denied that after registration of sale deed dated 18-2-73 Annexure-'D' the petitioners mutated their names with Rajuk and other authorities as would be evident from Memo dated 2-5-73, 2-10-88 vide Annexures E, E-1 and E-2, and that the petitioners applied to the Rajuk for permission to mortgage the property for securing loan from Pubali Bank, Motijheel Branch, Dhaka which was allowed vide Memo dated 21-11-80 Annexure-F and that the petitioners have been in possession of the property by paying taxes revenues, etc. without any interruption from any quarter whatsoever, and that for the first time they came to know that their property had been listed in 'Kha' list as abandoned property when they filed application for partition of the plot in April 1986. From these admitted facts without going into further details we also find that the property in question has been illegally listed in 'Kha' list as it does not come within the mischief of any provision of 16 of 1972 or Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 and of no legal effect.

64. In view of the discussions and decisions referred above we are of the view that each case is to be decided on the facts and circumstances on merits and we find that this instant Writ Petition No. 1472 of 1996 on its facts and circumstances is quite maintainable without availing the alternative forum. We also find that without forming an opinion, in view of section 5 of the Ordinance, the inclusion of the property as abandoned is absolutely illegal and without any lawful authority and this has been consistently found by both the Divisions of this court in many cases.

In the result the Rule is made absolute without cost. The inclusion of the property in question is hereby declared illegal and without any lawful authority and of no legal effect. The respondents are directed to exclude the property from 'Kha' list within 60 (sixty) days from the date of receipt of this order.

End.
